claims.claim: Negotiation is a discussion aimed at reaching an agreement; Fisher, Ury, and Patton (Getting to Yes) define it as back-and-forth communication designed to reach an agreement when the sides have some interests that are shared and others that are opposed.
Negotiation happens in everyday and workplace settings: job offers and salaries, supplier contracts, workplace conflicts, and purchases such as haggling over a car's price.
A position is what a side says it wants, while an interest is the underlying need behind the demand; Getting to Yes teaches negotiators to explore the interests underlying stated positions.
Distributive negotiation is hard bargaining over a fixed amount in which any gain for one side is a loss for the other; CFI gives the example of negotiating a car's price at a dealership.
Integrative negotiation attempts to create value so that both parties can achieve a win-win outcome, and it works by recognizing that each party values various outcomes differently.
Before a negotiation begins, a party should assess what it is seeking and what the other party is seeking; understanding both sides' desires is what makes a win-win outcome possible.

A BATNA (best alternative to a negotiated agreement) is the fallback available if talks fail; Fisher, Ury, and Patton call a strong BATNA the negotiator's greatest source of power, and wise negotiators improve it in advance (job hunters follow other leads, buyers talk to sellers' competitors).
Negotiations generally follow a process of discussion, clarification, negotiating an outcome, and agreement (CFI); this lesson restates that flow in plain language as open, explore, propose, agree.

Negotiating is a recognized management competency: OPM's Guide to the SES Qualifications lists Influencing/Negotiating — persuading others, building consensus through give and take, and gaining cooperation — among the executive core qualification competencies.

A deal the other side cannot live with tends to fail: CFI warns that pursuing only your own gain creates hostility and reduces the chance the outcome lasts, and OPM frames negotiating as consensus through give and take.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is negotiation inherently win-lose or win-win?
positions: Distributive accounts treat negotiation as a contest over a fixed pie in which one side's gain is the other's loss (CFI's hard-bargaining description).
Integrative accounts treat negotiation as joint problem-solving that can create value for both sides (CFI's win-win description; Getting to Yes's interest-based approach via PON).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches both forms as real, notes that most negotiations mix them, and adds the honest framing that even a distributive win only lasts if the other side can live with the deal.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Should a negotiator aim to maximize their own outcome or to satisfy both sides?
positions: Hard-bargaining advice pushes the negotiator to press for maximum personal gain.
Getting to Yes (via PON) and CFI warn that one-sided outcomes breed hostility and unravel.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson adopts the both-sides-can-live-with standard as its reality check, grounded in CFI's hostility warning and OPM's give-and-take competency definition.

correctionsNeeded: The phase-1 generated draft (if any) was treated as editorial intent only and fully rewritten; no unsupported claims carried over.
rightsIssues: PON and CFI are copyrighted web publications used reference-only (facts restated in original prose; the one-sentence Getting to Yes definition quoted with attribution).
OPM's Guide to the SES Qualifications is a U.S. government work (public domain).

sourceRecords.title: What Is Negotiation? (Program on Negotiation, Harvard Law School)
sourceRecords.provider: Program on Negotiation at Harvard Law School
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-22. University-program educational page (Tier A). Quotes Fisher, Ury, and Patton's Getting to Yes definition of negotiation as back-and-forth communication designed to reach an agreement when the sides have some interests that are shared and others that are opposed; 'everyone negotiates something every day'; and everyday settings including job offers, car prices, supplier contracts, and workplace conflict. Supports the working definition, the when-it-happens list, and the shared-and-opposed-interests framing. The one-sentence definition is quoted with attribution; everything else paraphrased.

sourceRecords.title: Principled Negotiation: Focus on Interests to Create Value (Program on Negotiation, Harvard Law School)
sourceRecords.provider: Program on Negotiation at Harvard Law School
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-22. University-program educational page (Tier A). States that principled negotiation, as described in Getting to Yes, encourages negotiators to share and explore the deeper interests underlying their stated positions. Supports the positions-versus-interests distinction and the interest-based path to agreement; also frames the third path beyond hard-line versus accommodating approaches.

sourceRecords.title: Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement (BATNA): Beyond the Basics (Program on Negotiation, Harvard Law School)
sourceRecords.provider: Program on Negotiation at Harvard Law School
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-22. University-program educational page (Tier A). Reports Fisher, Ury, and Patton (Getting to Yes) on BATNA: a strong BATNA is often the negotiator's greatest source of power, and wise negotiators determine and improve their back-up plan before and during negotiation (job hunters follow other leads; buyers talk to suppliers' competitors). Also discusses the no-deal option framing. Supports the preparation practice (target, walk-away, alternatives).

sourceRecords.title: What is Negotiation? (Corporate Finance Institute)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-22. Tier B educational explainer. Defines negotiation as a dialogue between two or more parties with the intention of reaching a mutually beneficial outcome or resolving a conflict; describes the general process (discussion, clarification, negotiating an outcome, agreement); advises assessing what you are seeking and what the other party is seeking; warns that seeking only your own gain creates hostility and reduces the chance of keeping the outcome. Supports the definition, the four-step process restatement, preparation, and the honest framing.

sourceRecords.title: Negotiation Tactics (Corporate Finance Institute)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-22. Tier B educational explainer. Describes the forms of negotiation: distributive negotiation as hard-bargaining over a fixed amount where any gain for one party is at the expense of the other (example: negotiating a car's price at a dealership), and integrative negotiation as a merit-based approach that appreciates that parties value outcomes differently and often aims for a win-win. Supports the distributive-versus-integrative distinction.

sourceRecords.title: Guide to the Senior Executive Service Qualifications (September 2012)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A government source. Read via Wayback Machine capture of the canonical OPM URL (web.archive.org/web/20251111020538/, 2025-11-11) because opm.gov's current Executive Core Qualifications page uses the revised 2023 framework that no longer names the competency. The 2012 Guide lists Influencing/Negotiating among the Building Coalitions ECQ competencies: persuades others; builds consensus through give and take; gains cooperation from others to obtain information and accomplish goals. Supports the claim that negotiating is a recognized management competency and the give-and-take framing. U.S. government work, public domain.
